Any dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach, termination, or invalidity thereof (each, a “Dispute”) shall first be referred by the Parties to their respective senior-level executives, or their designecs, {or attempted resolution through good faith negotiations. The presiding mediator shall have experience with disputes involving the technology that is the subjcct matter of this Agreement, The mediation shall be conducted in the English language and all mediation sessions shall be held in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Parties shall each be responsible for one-half of any fees or other amounts payable to the AAA or the mediator, and each Party shal} bear its own attorneys’ fees and other expenses in connection with the mediation, If efforts at mediation are unsuccessful in resolving the Dispute within thirly (30) days after the first mediation session, either Party may pursue any and all legal or equitable remedies available to it, subject to the remaining provisions of this Agreement. The Parties agree that the procedures set forth in this paragraph shall be the sole and exclusive means of resolving any and all Disputes. 17	```
18	The Defendants contend that the Complaint should be dismissed in its entirety for failure to comply with the 2004 Agreement’s dispute resolution and mediation clause. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. The clause provides that “[a]ny dispute, controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach, termination, or invalidity thereof shall first be referred by the parties to their senior-level executives for attempted resolution through good-faith negotiations.” Compl. Ex. A § 9.1 (emphasis added). Should negotiations fail, thirty days after making a written request to initiate those negotiations, “either Party may, by written notice to the other, require that the Dispute be referred to non-binding mediation administered by the American Arbitration Association.” Id. (emphasis added). The Defendants assert that Skold did not refer a dispute to a senior-level executive for negotiations and failed to make a written request that the dispute be referred to nonbinding mediation. L.P./Inc. Mot. to Dismiss at 12-13. Skold responds that the language of the mediation clause is permissive (“either Party may ... require”) and also argues that, in any event, Inc. has waived its right to invoke the clause because it participated in litigation over the dispute in the cancellation action before the TTAB. See Pl.’s L.P./Inc. Opp’n at 14-15.
19	The dispute resolution clause in the 2004 Agreement contains two clauses, one of which is mandatory (the parties shall refer the matter to senior executives to attempt to negotiate a resolution) and the other which is permissive (the parties may refer the matter to nonbinding mediation). Given the voluntary nature of the latter, this Court agrees with Skold that he was not required to refer this dispute to mediation before bringing suit here against Inc.
20	L.P. and S.A., who are not parties to the 2004 Agreement, also contend that the dispute resolution clause requires their dismissal from this action. In essence, they urge this Court to accept the contention that a nonparty to an agreement should be permitted to force a signatory party to engage in negotiations pursuant to a permissive mediation clause in that agreement as a condition precedent to filing suit but cite no relevant case or statute in support of this contention. See United States v. Benish, 5 F.3d 20, 26 (3d Cir.1993) (rejecting a party’s claim where the party “provided] no legal support for his argument or any persuasive reason” for the court to find in his favor). The Court sees no persuasive reason to dismiss Skold’s entire Complaint based on this unsupported argument. Accordingly, the motion to dismiss the Complaint against L.P. and S.A. on this ground shall be denied.
21	Regarding Inc.: although Skold did fail to bring in a senior-level executive to try to resolve the dispute — as he was required to do under the dispute resolution provision — Inc.’s participation in the TTAB proceedings waived any rights it may have had to seek to have the parties’ executives negotiate an end to the dispute. See, e.g., LBL Skysystems (USA), Inc. v. APG-Am., Inc., No. 02-5379, 2005 WL 2140240, at *30 (E.D.Pa. Aug. 31, 2005) (holding that a “party that engages in discovery and files pretrial motions waives a contract’s alternative dispute resolution provision”); Smith v. IMG Worldwide, Inc., 360 F.Supp.2d 681, 687 (E.D.Pa.2005) (finding that a party’s engaging in motion practice and providing “substantial discovery” constituted waiver of contractual alternative dispute resolution provision).
22	Viewing the four years’ worth of docket entries in the TTAB action, the Court considers that Inc. did not file a motion to stay the TTAB proceedings pending executive-level negotiations and instead filed, inter alia, motions to dismiss, a protective order, multiple summary judgment motions (one of which was partially granted in its favor), and a final brief in preparation for trial. See, e.g., Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897, 2012 WL 5902083 (T.T.A.B. Nov. 8, 2012) (granting Inc.’s motion for partial summary judgment on Skold’s abandonment claim). See also generally Registrant’s Trial Brief, Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897 (T.T.A.B. Aug. 13, 2014), Docket No. 81. This four-year history of litigation in the cancellation action — from filing nearly through trial — is, on its face, inconsistent with the notion that Inc. was willing to engage in the good-faith executive-level negotiations required by the dispute resolution provision.
23	Moreover, the Court can look to the TTAB’s grant of partial summary judgment in favor of Inc. and dismissing Skold’s abandonment claim as a concrete example of an instance where Inc.’s conduct inconsistent with the dispute resolution clause caused prejudice to Skold, not to mention the expenditure of time, cost, and resources attendant to maintaining a multi-year trademark cancellation action. The Defendants have undisputedly accepted the judicial process and have demonstrated that fact by: (1) Inc.’s failure to raise the issue of good-faith negotiations promptly before the TTAB; (2) Inc.’s engaging in discovery in the TTAB action; (3) Inc.’s filing of several pretrial motions in the TTAB action, none of which raise the issue of negotiation; and (4) the Defendants’ decision to wait until the case was ready to proceed to trial before the TTAB and until a Complaint was filed in this Court before asserting Skold’s failure to negotiate as grounds for a motion to dismiss. See St. Clair Area Sch. Dist. Bd. of Educ. v. E.I. Assocs., 733 A.2d 677, 682 n. 6 (Pa.Commw.Ct.1999) (“The key to determining whether [an alternative dispute resolution procedure] has been waived is whether the party, by virtue of its conduct, has accepted the judicial process.”). Inc. cannot now attempt to stand on the alternative dispute resolution clause as a reason for dismissal. Its right to invoke the clause has been waived.
24	```

Such examination shall be conducted, and CoJlaGenex shall make its records available, during normal business hours, after at least fifteen (15) days prior written notice to CollaGenex, as applicable, and shall take place at the facility(ies) where such records are maintained. Each such examination shall be limited to pertinent books and records for any year ending not more than twenty-four (24) months prior to the date of request; provided that Skold shall not be permitted to audit the same period of time more than once. Before permitting such independent accounting lirm to have access to such books and records, CollaGenex may require such independent accounting firm and its personnel involved in such audit, to signa confidentiality agreement (in form and substance reasonably acceptable to CollaGenex) as to any confidential information which is to be provided to such accounting firm or to which such accounting firm will have access, while conducting the audit under this paragraph. The Skold independent accounting firm will prepare and provide to each Party a writlen report stating whether the royalties and Sublicense Income payment reports submitted and royaltics and Subliccnse Income payments paid are correct or incorrect and the details concerning any discrepancies. Such accounting firm may not reveal to Skold any information leamed in the course of such audit other than the amount of any such discrepancies. Skold agrees to hold in stnct confidence all information disclosed to it, except to the extent necessary for Skold to enforce its rights under this Agreement or if disclosure is required by law. In the event there was an underpayment by CollaGenex hereunder, CollaGenex shall promptly (but in no event later than thirty (30) days after such Party’s receipt of the independent auditor’s report so correctly concluding) make payment to Skold of any shortfall. In the event that there was an overpayment by CollaGenex hereunder, Skold shall promptly (but in no event later than thirty (30) days after Skold’s receipt of the independent auditor’s report so correctly concluding) refund to CollaGenex or credit to future royalties, at ColljaGenex’s election, the excess amount. 2	
3	Contract `93FSupp3d375_personal_deposit_account_agreement`, filed in 93 F.Supp.3d 375. The full text is in `contract.txt` beside this file — read it if you want to see what the construed provision sits next to.

8	
9	"Part I — International ACH and Wire Transactions (NACHA Operating Rules)"  (risk type: 1.3)
10	
11	```
12	International ACH and Wire Transactions If your Account receives incoming ACH transactions (either credits or debits) or wire transfers initiated from outside of the United States, both you and we are subject to the Operating Rules and Guidelines of the National Automated Clearing House Association (“NACHA”) or the rules of any wire transfer system involved, and the laws enforced by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (“OFAC”). Under such rules and laws, we may temporarily suspend processing of a transaction for greater scrutiny or verification against the OFAC list of blocked parties, which may result in delayed settlement, posting and/or availability of funds. If we determine there is a violation, or if we cannot satisfactorily resolve a suspected or potential violation, the subject funds will be blocked as required by law. If you believe you have adequate grounds to seek the return of any blocked funds, it is your sole responsibility to pursue the matter with the appropriate governmental authorities. Please see the OFAC website for procedures and form required to seek a release of blocked funds.
13	```

16	
17	```
18	The bulk of Plaintiffs’ breach claim centers around their argument that TD’s conduct violated the NACHA Rules, which Plaintiffs claim were incorporated into the Account Agreement. See Compl. at ¶ 166-67. In order to address this claim we must first determine whether the NACHA rules were in fact incorporated. In support of this point, Plaintiffs cite to page 16 of the Account Agreement, which states in relevant part:

Taking the Plaintiffs’ allegations as true, the Complaint raises a plausible claim that some number of the loans originated outside of the United States. 18	The more significant problem with Love-joy’s argument that it had an “unfettered” right to redefine the House Accounts is that this interpretation would nullify portions of the Agreement’s termination provision. PL’s Opp. Br. at 17. Under the termination provision, the Agreement became effective January 1, 2004, and:
19	shall continue in force for a one (1) year period, and shall be automatically renewed for additional one (1) year periods thereafter unless terminated by written notice from either party to the other party not less than sixty (60) days prior to the end of the initial or any subsequent one (1) year term.

The Agreement also provides for termination by either party under certain additional circumstances, including (1) a change of 50% or more of the ownership of the other party; (2) the other party’s unreasonable and repeated failure to perform the terms and conditions of the Agreement; or (3) the other party’s filing of a bankruptcy petition. Id. Finally, the Agreement expressly contemplates that the parties could terminate the Agreement at any time by “mutual written agreement.” Id.
21	The termination provision, on its face, provides a comprehensive account of the ways in which the Agreement may be terminated. There is no indication in the Agreement that the parties contemplated that the House Accounts provision would constitute an additional means for terminating all of Lovejoy’s obligations under the Agreement. Under Lovejoy’s construction of the House Accounts provision, however, Lovejoy could, at any time and without Kamco’s consent, redefine every single account in Kamco’s territory as a House Account. This interpretation would allow Lovejoy to escape from all of its obligations under the Agreement and all of the restrictions in the termination provision.
22	This reading is inconsistent with Pennsylvania law, which, as noted above, forbids courts from “interpreting] one provision of a contract in a manner which results in another portion being annulled,” LJL Transp., 962 A.2d at 648 (citation omitted), and requires that “[t]he whole instrument ... be taken together in arriving at contractual intent,” Duquesne Univ., 777 A.2d at 429 (citation omitted). In other words, the “mutual” termination provision would never apply to Lovejoy.

This purpose would obviously be frustrated if one party maintained a unilateral right to opt out of all of its obligations under the contract at any time — which is precisely how Lovejoy construes the House Accounts provision.
24	This court’s conclusion that Lovejoy’s reading of the House Accounts provision is inconsistent with the parties’ intent is reinforced by the fact that the Agreement contains a non-compete provision. The noncompetition provision states that Kamco could not, without Lovejoy’s permission, sell any product which is directly competitive with any Lovejoy product that Kamco was supposed to sell on Lovejoy’s behalf. Id. ¶ 2. If, as Lovejoy suggests, the House Accounts provision granted Lovejoy the “unfettered” right to redefine all or substantially all accounts as House Accounts, then Lovejoy would have the unilateral power to deprive Kamco of all of the benefits it was to receive under the contract while simultaneously barring Kamco from selling any product made by a Lovejoy competitor. Pearle Vision Center, Inc., 376 Pa.Super. 580, 546 A.2d 676, 679 (1988); see also Duquesne Light, 66 F.3d at 617 (noting that “courts generally utilize the good faith duty as an interpretive tool to determine the parties’ justifiable expectations”). Reading the House Accounts provision in this manner allows the termination provision to have its intended effect: If one of the parties wishes to put an end to its obligations to the other party, it must follow one of the enumerated ways of terminating the Agreement.

{"clause_id":"c020","reasoning_cat1":"Two dated periods stated precisely; no ambiguous term.","reasoning_cat2":"The one-month extension interacts with the 'Policy Year' definition (c056), which provides that any extension forms part of the Policy Year that would have ended on the original expiration date, and with the Discovery Period deeming rule in c037.","prob_cat1":0.10,"prob_cat2":0.29},

{"clause_id":"c025","reasoning_cat1":"A list of named entities with a scanning typo ('Fisst Federal'); the substitution itself is definite.","reasoning_cat2":"Because 'Named Insured' means the first entity listed in Item 1 (c053), placing Vantus Bank first silently changes who receives notice, cancels and acts for all Insureds under c105, c115 and c104.","prob_cat1":0.16,"prob_cat2":0.33},
{"clause_id":"c026","reasoning_cat1":"A list of form numbers; nothing intrinsically uncertain.","reasoning_cat2":"It conflicts in content with the Item 13 lists in c017 and c021, so the governing endorsement schedule is version-dependent.","prob_cat1":0.11,"prob_cat2":0.28},

{"clause_id":"c031","reasoning_cat1":"A definite condition precedent to any Insuring Agreement operating; no vague term.","reasoning_cat2":"It duplicates Item 6 (c014) and governs the endorsement Insuring Agreements (c128, c145, c165), all of which have Item 6 entries, so no inconsistency appears.","prob_cat1":0.11,"prob_cat2":0.26},
{"clause_id":"c032","reasoning_cat1":"The carve-out 'except for Loss the Company pays as indemnification' is a short phrase that decides whether A-side coverage is displaced, and 'pays' sits uneasily against the presumptive-indemnification concept used elsewhere.","reasoning_cat2":"Section VII(B)(2) (c091) and Section VIII(A)(2) (c093) apply the (B) retention whether or not indemnification is actually granted, which pulls in a different direction from a carve-out keyed to what the Company actually pays.","prob_cat1":0.31,"prob_cat2":0.37},
{"clause_id":"c033","reasoning_cat1":"'has agreed to or is legally permitted or required by law to indemnify' is the standard but genuinely contested trigger for B-side coverage.","reasoning_cat2":"It must be squared with the retention rules in c091 and the order-of-payments provision in c094; the fit is workable but the permitted/required distinction recurs.","prob_cat1":0.24,"prob_cat2":0.26},
{"clause_id":"c034","reasoning_cat1":"A short grant of entity coverage for Wrongful Acts; the heading is garbled ('es') but the operative words are plain.","reasoning_cat2":"Its scope is cut down by the Securities Liability Exclusion (c124), the Item 6 note in c015 and the Section VI exclusions (c079-c089), so its practical reach depends on other provisions.","prob_cat1":0.13,"prob_cat2":0.25},
{"clause_id":"c035","reasoning_cat1":"The enumeration is garbled ('a)' paired with '(2)'), and the final sentence's exclusion of loss 'arising from any act or omission by' the estate or spouse could swallow much of the grant.","reasoning_cat2":"It coheres with the Insured Person definition (c048) and the Wrongful Act definition (c061); no direct conflict located.","prob_cat1":0.22,"prob_cat2":0.14},
{"clause_id":"c036","reasoning_cat1":"'at the direction of the Company' and the excess-of-other-indemnification proviso are the kind of short qualifiers that can be read two ways, but the provision is otherwise plain.","reasoning_cat2":"This subsection is deleted for three of the five purchased coverages (c130, c147, c167), so its survival is patchy across the instrument, and it overlaps the excess clause in c118.","prob_cat1":0.17,"prob_cat2":0.31},
{"clause_id":"c037","reasoning_cat1":"The trigger is limited to cancellation, nonrenewal or conversion 'subject to Section XIII (C)(1)(b)', and the bar on notice of circumstances during the Discovery Period is a hard rule with significant consequences; several phrases here are worth fighting over.","reasoning_cat2":"Section XIII(C)(2) (c106) says the occurrence of ANY of the conversion events — including Financial Impairment under (C)(1)(a) — shall not affect the right to purchase the Discovery Period, which cannot be squared with this section's limitation to (C)(1)(b).","prob_cat1":0.38,"prob_cat2":0.56},
{"clause_id":"c038","reasoning_cat1":"'all applications, attachments and materials submitted to the Insurer' for this or any predecessor policy is a sweeping and boundary-less description of the incorporated documents.","reasoning_cat2":"It sits against the entire-agreement clause (c113) and the representations/severability provisions (c109-c111), which turn on what the Application contained.","prob_cat1":0.24,"prob_cat2":0.25},
{"clause_id":"c039","reasoning_cat1":"A defined-term list closing with broad additions ('economic advice, financial advice', 'financial planning advice including without limitation') and then carve-outs, which is exactly the general-versus-specific structure that produces scope fights.","reasoning_cat2":"It drives both the Section V(B) exclusion (c064) and the Brokerage Insuring Agreement (c128), so the same words both grant and exclude coverage depending on the endorsement.","prob_cat1":0.28,"prob_cat2":0.22},
{"clause_id":"c040","reasoning_cat1":"'a written or oral demand for monetary damages or non-monetary relief' is a notoriously contested formulation, and the trailing qualifier 'for a Wrongful Act including any appeal from such proceeding' attaches unclearly to the whole list.","reasoning_cat2":"The definition governs the notice provisions (c097, c098), the single-claim rule (c092) and the Discovery Period reporting rule (c037), so its boundaries have knock-on effects throughout.","prob_cat1":0.33,"prob_cat2":0.27},
{"clause_id":"c041","reasoning_cat1":"A one-line statutory definition; nothing to construe.","reasoning_cat2":"Used only in c160; consistent.","prob_cat1":0.03,"prob_cat2":0.03},
{"clause_id":"c042","reasoning_cat1":"Definite in structure, though it fixes Subsidiary status by reference to the inception date and then admits later bank Subsidiaries only 'subject to Section XII (B)'.","reasoning_cat2":"It is replaced for the Discovery Period by c005 and depends on Section XII(B), which the Mergers Endorsement rewrites (c180) and the Discovery Period endorsement deletes altogether (c006).","prob_cat1":0.21,"prob_cat2":0.42},
{"clause_id":"c043","reasoning_cat1":"'reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses' is a standard but genuinely elastic phrase, and the exclusion of 'overhead' has fuzzy edges.","reasoning_cat2":"It interacts with the advancement and allocation provisions (c096, c107, c108) which give the Insurer power to test reasonableness; the fit is coherent.","prob_cat1":0.24,"prob_cat2":0.20},
{"clause_id":"c044","reasoning_cat1":"The statute is misnamed ('Employment Retirement Income Security Act'), but the reference is unmistakable and the error does not change meaning.","reasoning_cat2":"Used in c067 and c145/c153; consistent throughout.","prob_cat1":0.12,"prob_cat2":0.05},
{"clause_id":"c045","reasoning_cat1":"The definition excepts 'Leased Employee or Independent Contractor' in capitalised form, yet neither is defined anywhere, leaving the carve-out's boundary unfixed.","reasoning_cat2":"Section IV contains no definition of either capitalised term, so the exception cannot be resolved from the rest of the instrument, and Employee feeds the Insured Person definition (c048) and the Fiduciary endorsement definitions (c149-c151).","prob_cat1":0.28,"prob_cat2":0.27},
{"clause_id":"c046","reasoning_cat1":"The definition is closed and specific — appointment of a receiver or similar official, or debtor in possession — with little room for argument on its face.","reasoning_cat2":"It is the hinge between the Insolvency Exclusion (c083), which excludes claims 'involving' Financial Impairment, and Section XVI(I) (c120), which says Financial Impairment shall not release the Insurer; those two pull in opposite directions.","prob_cat1":0.22,"prob_cat2":0.38},
{"clause_id":"c047","reasoning_cat1":"A two-element definition; nothing ambiguous on its face.","reasoning_cat2":"The Fiduciary endorsement replaces this definition (c152), so 'Insured' has two meanings depending on which coverage is engaged.","prob_cat1":0.07,"prob_cat2":0.19},
{"clause_id":"c048","reasoning_cat1":"'officer' and 'honorary or advisory director' are undefined and the class covers past, present and future persons, but the formulation is conventional.","reasoning_cat2":"Because 'Company' includes Subsidiaries (c042), the class of Insured Persons expands and contracts with c005 and c077; that interaction is workable but not trivial.","prob_cat1":0.24,"prob_cat2":0.23},
{"clause_id":"c049","reasoning_cat1":"A closed five-item list of services with no catch-all; comparatively tight drafting.","reasoning_cat2":"It drives the Section V(I) exclusion (c071) and its credit-life carve-out; consistent with c039's parallel carve-out.","prob_cat1":0.11,"prob_cat2":0.13},
{"clause_id":"c050","reasoning_cat1":"'common nexus any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction or series of related facts' is a relatedness formula that courts repeatedly find susceptible to competing readings of how loose the nexus may be.","reasoning_cat2":"It controls the single-claim rule (c092), the Prior Notice Exclusion (c074), the Subsidiary exclusion (c077) and c103, so a broad or narrow reading materially changes several other provisions.","prob_cat1":0.42,"prob_cat2":0.33}

{"judgments": [
{"clause_id":"c101","reasoning_cat1":"A structured consent-condition with a numerical threshold; the only softness is 'as soon as practicable' and the Insurer's 'sole discretion'.","reasoning_cat2":"The Mergers Endorsement (c179) deletes and replaces this subsection with a 20% threshold rather than 25%, and the Discovery Period endorsement deletes Section XII altogether (c006), so three documents give three answers.","prob_cat1":0.21,"prob_cat2":0.51},
{"clause_id":"c102","reasoning_cat1":"A short automatic-coverage grant keyed to a numerical asset test; definite on its face.","reasoning_cat2":"It is replaced by c180 (20% instead of 25%) and is the very provision the Company definition (c042) makes itself 'subject to', while c006 deletes Section XII entirely for the Discovery Period.","prob_cat1":0.16,"prob_cat2":0.49},
{"clause_id":"c103","reasoning_cat1":"The carve-out for anything 'arising out of or directly or indirectly resulting from' pre-acquisition Wrongful Acts is very wide, and limb (2) depends on the loose Interrelated Wrongful Acts test.","reasoning_cat2":"Section V(O) (c077) excepts claims 'as provided in Section XII (C)(3)', but this subsection has only limbs (1) and (2); and c181 preserves 'all other provisions of Section XII' while c006 deletes them.","prob_cat1":0.30,"prob_cat2":0.42},
{"clause_id":"c104","reasoning_cat1":"The three sentences on return premium are hard to reconcile with each other: a flat 90% rule, then a 90% rule for multi-year policies before the first anniversary, then pro rata afterwards, with no rule for a multi-year policy in year one that is not covered by the second sentence.","reasoning_cat2":"Item 10(b) shows three-year pre-paid premiums, so the multi-year branch is live, and the Discovery Period fully-earned rules (c007, c037) and c106(2) further restrict cancellation.","prob_cat1":0.30,"prob_cat2":0.30},
{"clause_id":"c105","reasoning_cat1":"Clear notice mechanics with two defined notice periods; nothing intrinsically uncertain.","reasoning_cat2":"The Iowa Amendatory Endorsement (c187) deletes and replaces this very subsection with a different and longer scheme, so the printed text is superseded but still appears in the instrument.","prob_cat1":0.15,"prob_cat2":0.46},
{"clause_id":"c106","reasoning_cat1":"'the Company ceasing to engage actively in its primary business' is a vague trigger for cutting off coverage, and 'acquisition of substantially all of the assets' imports another elastic standard.","reasoning_cat2":"Subsection (2) preserves the Discovery Period right on the occurrence of ANY of the three conversion events, but Section III (c037) confers that right only where the Policy converts 'subject to Section XIII (C)(1)(b)' — a direct inconsistency that matters where Financial Impairment under (C)(1)(a) occurs.","prob_cat1":0.33,"prob_cat2":0.52},
{"clause_id":"c107","reasoning_cat1":"Allocation 'based on the relative legal exposures of the parties' is a standard whose application is inherently contestable, and limb (1)(a) deems 100% of joint non-defence Loss to be the Insured Persons' while (1)(b) allocates 'all other Loss', which is hard to square.","reasoning_cat2":"It works with the arbitration machinery in c108 and the retention rules in c091, but the 100% deeming in (1)(a) pulls against the Insurer's 100% payment obligation in c091(B)(4) and the order of payments in c094.","prob_cat1":0.36,"prob_cat2":0.31},
{"clause_id":"c108","reasoning_cat1":"Arbitration is available only 'if requested by the Insured' and only for Defense Costs allocation, and the Insurer need advance only what it 'believes to be covered' — permissive and self-judging language of the kind courts have had to parse.","reasoning_cat2":"The advancement standard here is weaker than the unqualified advancement duty in c096(1), which is expressly made 'Subject to Section XIV', so the two provisions must be read together to know what is actually owed.","prob_cat1":0.30,"prob_cat2":0.28},
{"clause_id":"c109","reasoning_cat1":"Limb (1) says the Application is construed as a separate application by each Insured Person while limb (2) says the Policy is not a series of individual contracts — two statements pulling in opposite directions within one clause.","reasoning_cat2":"That tension carries into the Severability provisions (c110, c111), which sever knowledge person by person yet deny coverage to the Company on senior officers' knowledge.","prob_cat1":0.31,"prob_cat2":0.34},
{"clause_id":"c110","reasoning_cat1":"Limbs (1)-(3) key rescission to who 'knew' of undisclosed facts, but the closing sentence says the conditions apply 'whether or not the Insured Person actually knew if the misrepresentation ... was made' — a sentence that both is garbled and appears to undo the knowledge requirement.","reasoning_cat2":"It sits against the Severability of Exclusions provision (c111), which forbids imputing one Insured Person's knowledge to another, and against c109(1)'s separate-application rule.","prob_cat1":0.44,"prob_cat2":0.36},
